title: When Decisions Arent Reversible
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece revisits Jeff Bezos's well-known distinction between one-way and two-way decisions at Amazon, using it to argue that organizations should not apply a single decision-making process to every choice. One-way, hard-to-reverse decisions deserve slow, deliberate analysis, while two-way, reversible decisions should be delegated quickly to subject-matter experts to keep the organization nimble. The author warns that treating all decisions with the same heavy process breeds bureaucracy and slows down routine choices unnecessarily, and recommends reserving rigorous deliberation exclusively for genuinely consequential, hard-to-undo decisions.
points: Jeff Bezos's distinction between one-way and two-way decisions is presented as a useful decision-making framework.
One-way, hard-to-reverse decisions warrant slow, deliberate, well-resourced processes.
Two-way, reversible decisions should be pushed down to subject-matter experts and made quickly.
Applying a single heavyweight process to all decisions creates bureaucracy that slows the whole organization.
quotes: One-way decisions are those choices that can’t be easily reversed.
Two-way decisions, on the other hand, are those choices that, if need be, can be changed or altered.
By applying a full-blown decision process to all decisions, leaders gum up the works.
By increasing the ownership and autonomy around two-way decisions, leaders empower team members and trust them.
An organization that can’t decide the everyday choice with speed soon becomes bogged down by bureaucracy and red tape.
